Following a recent "2+2" consultation in Cairo, the two countries issued a joint statement emphasizing their water security as "indivisible" and warning that Ethiopia's unilateral actions threaten downstream water availability. They called for a binding legal framework and negotiations based on international law, rejecting any involvement from other Nile Basin nations. Ethiopia, which inaugurated the GERD in September 2025, argues that the dam is crucial for its development and does not infringe on the water rights of downstream countries. The historical 1959 Nile Waters Agreement, which allocated water without Ethiopia's participation, is contested by Ethiopia, which insists on equitable use of shared resources. Tensions have escalated as Egypt and Sudan seek to strengthen their diplomatic coordination against Ethiopia's development plans.

ethiopia.title: Deadly RSF drone attacks reveal deep divisions between Sudan and Ethiopia - Al Jazeera
ethiopia.content: Deadly RSF drone attacks reveal deep divisions between Sudan and Ethiopia | Border Disputes News | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Middle East Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Explained Sport Opinion Video Interactives More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up Navigation menu caret-left US-Israel war on Iran Yemen conflict Middle East Africa Asia Asia Pacific Europe Latin America US & Canada caret-right News | Border Disputes Deadly RSF drone attacks reveal deep divisions between Sudan and Ethiopia Deadly drone attacks in Sudan have led to fierce diplomatic disputes with Ethiopia, exposing complex regional rivalries and fragile border security. Listen Listen (6 mins) Save Share Deadly RSF drone attacks reveal deep divisions between Sudan and Ethiopia on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Rubble left after fires at Alneam market after a drone attack in the disputed Abyei region along the border between South Sudan and Sudan, October 20, 2026 [Handout via Reuters] By Mohammad Mansour Published On 3 Nov 2026 3 Nov 2026 The Sudanese government’s allegations that Ethiopia is behind a deadly wave of unmanned aerial assaults belie a deep and longstanding rift between the two countries, which threatens to intensify internal conflicts in both. Sudan has officially lodged complaints with the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council over allegations that the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary – which has been at war with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) since April 2023 – is using Ethiopian territory to launch attacks against civilian sites, including power stations. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 As aid situation worsens, displaced Sudanese worry about warnings of famine list 2 of 3 Sudan files complaints against Ethiopia with UN over deadly drone spree list 3 of 3 Drone attacks extend campaign targeting Sudan’s power system end of list Ethiopia’s alleged support for the RSF has triggered differences within the SAF on how to respond next, Sudanese border affairs specialist Abdul Kareem Al-Almin Ahmed told Al Jazeera. “The mutual accusations are many and almost daily, and the tension on the part of the Sudanese army has reached high levels, to the degree that made some voices inside the Sudanese army and the forces allied with it demand that Sudan declare war on Ethiopia based on these interventions,” Al-Almin told Al Jazeera. Suspected RSF drone attacks have heavily damaged civilian infrastructure in SAF-controlled areas. More than 90 percent of power stations in Sudanese cities have been rendered out of service due to drone attacks, and al-Almin said the technological capabilities of these weapons indicate significant external backing. “They are mysterious drones, drones that reach long distances, and almost all Sudanese lands are currently violated by these drones, which confirms that they are drones with a special characteristic and flight properties for a long range and have high destructive power,” Al-Almin added. A detailed report prepared by the Sudanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs alongside military intelligence claimed that 70 separate assaults involving 187 one-way attack drones were launched from Ethiopian territory between February and October. The frequency of these attacks seems to be increasing, with 28 attacks carried out by 97 drones in October. Advertisement The use of armed drones has been catastrophic for civilians in Sudan, with 13 million people already displaced and thousands at risk of famine due to the war. Between February 15 and October 27, drone attacks killed 176 Sudanese soldiers and 484 civilians, according to a report compiled by the Transitional Sovereignty Council, which is linked to the de facto Sudanese leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the SAF. It identified Asosa Airport in western Ethiopia, the Kurmuk-Gizen border area, and the Bahir Dar airbase in Amhara as specific launch sites for drone attacks. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Saturday he was appalled by the use of drones in the war and condemned the catastrophic toll this was having on civilians. A drone attack on displaced families in Wad el-Mahi , near the Ethiopian border on October 3, killed 26 women and four children. Another drone attack in Nyala, in Sudan’s Darfur region, on October 26 killed at least 21 people and injured at least 40. The Sudanese military has repeatedly accused the Ethiopian government of aiding the RSF. Addis Ababa denies the claims and has in turn accused the Sudanese government of backing rebels linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front . The tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia extend beyond these drone attacks and allegations of support for rebel groups. They also involve a confrontation over water resources and strategic regional alliances. There have been ongoing tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), built by Addis Ababa on the Nile River. Egypt and Sudan rely heavily on the Nile for water supplies and, being downstream, fear the GERD threatens their national security and claim it breaches international law. “The Sudanese-Ethiopian file is a complex file, in which many factors have intertwined: The Renaissance Dam problem first … and the rapprochement between the Sudanese army and the Egyptian government,” Al-Almin said. The Sudanese government is also angered that the RSF is allegedly receiving support from Ethiopia, he added. But Badr Hassan Al-Shafei, a professor of African studies and conflict resolution expert, said fears of an escalation that could harm Sudan and Ethiopia are preventing an all-out confrontation between the two countries. In a study published by the Al Jazeera Centre for Studies, Al-Shafei wrote that “Khartoum’s interest lies in the stability of its eastern neighbourhood to avoid security threats and waves of asylum. “Khartoum fears that providing military support to Tigray will lead to an explosion of the situation on its borders, which may increase displacement operations that the border Sudanese states cannot bear, especially in light of the continuation of the war against Hemedti,” Al-Shafei stated. Advertisement A direct military confrontation with Addis Ababa would severely strain an already exhausted Sudanese military apparatus, which is still involved in intense battles with the RSF in the southeast of the country. Ultimately, leaders of both countries recognise the catastrophic potential of expanding the battlefield beyond each other’s borders. “If the Sudanese army opens a war front with Ethiopia, this is not in its favour and confuses the region,” Al-Amin wrote. “[Sudan could find itself] fighting on two fronts: Fighting the Rapid Support Forces that occupy part of Sudan, and fighting the Ethiopian army that possesses its capabilities and the border extension capable of reaching through it.” aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement About About Show more About Us Code of Ethics Terms and Conditions EU/EEA Regulatory Notice Privacy Policy Cookie Policy Cookie Preferences Accessibility Statement Sitemap Work for us Connect Connect Show more Contact Us User Accounts Help Advertise with us Stay Connected Newsletters Channel Finder TV Schedule Podcasts Submit a Tip Paid Partner Content Our Channels Our Channels Show more Al Jazeera Arabic Al Jazeera English Al Jazeera Investigative Unit Al Jazeera Mubasher Al Jazeera Documentary Al Jazeera Balkans AJ+ Our Network Our Network Show more Al Jazeera Centre for Studies Al Jazeera Media Institute Learn Arabic Al Jazeera Centre for Public Liberties & Human Rights Al Jazeera Forum Al Jazeera Hotel Partners Follow Al Jazeera English: facebook twitter youtube instagram-colored-outline rss bluesky tiktok-colored-outline © 2026 Al Jazeera Media Network
ethiopia.summary: Recent drone attacks attributed to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have heightened tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia, revealing deep-rooted divisions and escalating regional conflicts. Sudanese officials have accused Ethiopia of facilitating these attacks, which have targeted civilian infrastructure, including power stations, leading to significant damage and casualties. The Sudanese government has lodged complaints with the UN Security Council and the African Union, claiming that over 70 drone assaults were launched from Ethiopian territory between February and October 2026. The situation has prompted calls within Sudan's military for a potential declaration of war against Ethiopia. Despite the rising hostilities, experts suggest that both nations are wary of a full-scale confrontation due to the potential for further destabilization. The ongoing conflict is compounded by disputes over water resources related to the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, which has strained relations between Sudan, Ethiopia, and Egypt. The humanitarian impact is severe, with millions displaced and thousands facing famine.

somalia.content: Indian Navy Frees 20 Crew After Somalia Boat Hijacking — JournalArta Global Journal Arta ID EN · GLOBAL Tuesday, November 3, 2026 · Jakarta S&P 7,568.92 ▲0.36% USD/IDR 18,148 ▲0.19% Subscribe Journal Arta Global Edition beyond headlines Indonesia ▾ News Business Travel Culture Asia ▾ Southeast Asia East Asia South Asia World ▾ United States Europe Middle East Americas & Africa Business ▾ Companies Macro & Policy Energy Markets ▾ Stocks Crypto Forex & Commodities Technology ▾ AI Gadgets Apps & Software Gaming Sport ▾ Football Combat Sports Basketball More Sports Lifestyle ▾ Entertainment Travel Food & Health Shopping & Deals Search Advertisement Asia Asia · South Asia Indian Navy Frees 20 Crew After Somalia Boat Hijacking Twenty crew members are safe after Indian naval forces freed an Iranian fishing boat seized off Somalia, an incident that brought suspected pirates and Somali By Alistair Sterling November 3, 2026 2 min read Indian Navy Frees 20 Crew After Somalia Boat Hijacking Twenty crew members are safe after Indian naval forces freed an Iranian fishing boat seized off Somalia, an incident that brought suspected pirates and Somali security personnel ashore in the country’s northeast. The operation lasted more than 48 hours and ended in the Arabian Sea. India’s Defense Ministry announced the rescue Tuesday. Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said the crew’s boat, the Azini, was recovered Monday more than 3,000 kilometers (1,865 miles) from Mumbai. Suspects disarmed and released An official with the Puntland Maritime Police Force said Indian forces disarmed 12 suspected Somali pirates, took their mobile phones and then released them. The official spoke anonymously because he was not authorized to address the media. The suspects and two Somali security guards later reached Bandar Bayla, in northeastern Somalia, the official said. Three people who came ashore had minor injuries. The official did not identify whether they were among the suspected pirates or the guards, or explain how they were hurt. Advertisement India’s ministry said the operation concluded without casualties or injuries. The statement left unclear whether that description referred to everyone involved or only the rescued crew. What is known about the rescue The accounts confirm that the vessel had been hijacked off Somalia and that Indian forces freed the boat and its 20 crew. They do not describe how the navy found the Azini or the tactics used during the operation. The location of the hijacking and the identities of the suspected pirates were also not specified. Read also Ballot Scanner Failure Disrupts Voting in New York House Battleground That distinction matters: the Puntland official described 12 people as suspected pirates, while the Indian ministry reported the successful rescue. The claims about disarmament and the suspects’ release come from the local maritime police official; India’s account focused on the operation and its outcome. The incident involved a fishing vessel linked to Iran, Indian naval forces operating in the Arabian Sea and suspected Somali pirates who later landed in Puntland. For the crew, the immediate stakes were direct: their boat had been seized, and their release followed an operation that ran for more than two days. For authorities, the arrival of the suspects and guards at Bandar Bayla adds a local dimension to a rescue carried out at sea. Advertisement The reported details leave the crew’s condition central to what happens next. India’s ministry said there were no injuries, while the Puntland official separately reported minor injuries among three people who came ashore. He did not say whether those injured were guards or suspects. India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said the rescue was completed in the Arabian Sea, more than 3,000 kilometers from Mumbai. somalia.summary: The Indian Navy successfully rescued 20 crew members from an Iranian fishing boat, the Azini, that had been hijacked off the coast of Somalia. The operation, which lasted over 48 hours, concluded in the Arabian Sea, more than 3,000 kilometers from Mumbai. India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh confirmed the crew's safety following the rescue, which involved disarming 12 suspected Somali pirates. These suspects were subsequently released by Indian forces, along with their mobile phones, and later reached Bandar Bayla in northeastern Somalia. While the Indian Ministry reported no casualties during the operation, a Puntland Maritime Police official mentioned that three individuals who came ashore had minor injuries, though it was unclear whether they were pirates or security guards. The details surrounding the hijacking and the tactics used by the Indian Navy remain undisclosed, highlighting the complexities of maritime security in the region.

somalia.title: Somalia Produces Just 5% of Estimated Annual Fishery Capacity - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia Produces Just 5% of Estimated Annual Fishery Capacity - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia Produces Just 5% of Estimated Annual Fishery Capacity Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday November 3, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia produces about 30,000 tonnes of fish annually, just 5% of its estimated marine fishery production capacity of 600,000 tonnes, according to a report by The EastAfrican, as the country seeks to attract investment into its underdeveloped fishing industry. Abdi Dirshe, director general of Somalia's Ministry of Fisheries and Blue Economy, said the gap between current output and estimated capacity stands at nearly 570,000 tonnes a year. Dirshe estimated that the sector could generate between $1.8 billion and $3 billion in annual revenue and create more than 210,000 jobs if its resources were properly developed. The figures represent potential economic returns rather than existing industry revenue or employment. Somalia has approximately 3,333 kilometres of coastline, but inadequate fishing equipment, limited processing and storage facilities, and security concerns have restricted the industry's development. Investment and fisheries policy Expanding production would require investment in fishing vessels, equipment, landing sites, cold storage, processing plants and export infrastructure. Abdullahi Adan, coordinator of Somalia's Sustainable Fisheries Development Project, known as Badmaal, said the government's National Transformation Plan 2025–2029 prioritises private investment, market development and public-private partnerships in the sector. Somalia has introduced legal and regulatory measures intended to encourage investment, including an Investment Law, a public-private partnership policy, a Fisheries Law and food safety regulations. Local companies have also begun investing in fish processing and boatbuilding, with projects aimed at creating jobs and developing technical skills among young Somalis. Export markets and security challenges Engineer Ali Ibrahim Siyad, chairman of the Somali Fish Exporters Association, said quality assurance and seafood certification are essential for gaining access to international markets. He identified the United States, China, the Middle East and East African countries as potential destinations for Somali fish exports. However, exporters face difficulties meeting the requirements of international markets, while the industry continues to operate with limited infrastructure and equipment. Fisheries expert Omar Abdulle Hayle said security remains the primary consideration for investors seeking to protect their personnel and assets. The report also identified limited capacity to protect marine resources as an obstacle to developing the industry. Fisheries experts called for transparent management and stronger marine environmental protection alongside efforts to increase production. somalia.title: Somalia, Djibouti national security inseparable: Somali's parliament speaker - TRT Afrika
somalia.content: Somalia, Djibouti national security inseparable: Somali's parliament speaker - TRT Afrika | English | English POLITICS AFRICA TÜRKİYE OPINION FEATURES SPORTS AFRICA 6 min read Somalia, Djibouti national security inseparable: Somali's parliament speaker Somalia’s parliament speaker praises Djibouti’s role in the rebuilding of Somalia, from the historic Arta peace conference to its military contribution to the fight against terrorism. Share Somalia’s parliament speaker Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur with Djibouti President Ismail Omar Guelleh By Nuri Aden Somalia’s parliament speaker said Tuesday that the security of Somalia cannot be considered separately from the security of Djibouti, calling for closer cooperation between the two neighbours as the Horn of Africa faces growing security tensions. Speaker Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur said the two countries shared a responsibility to protect their peace and stability. He made the remarks in an address to Djibouti’s parliamentarians during his first official visit abroad since taking office . “Djibouti’s security is our security, and Somalia’s security is Djibouti’s security,” Nur told lawmakers. The peace and stability of our two countries are a shared responsibility in which we are equal partners.” The speaker, also known as Jaamac, made the visit at the invitation of his Djibouti counterpart, Dileita Mohamed Dileita. Nur described the relationship between the two countries as one that extended beyond diplomacy, pointing to their shared history, family ties and Djibouti’s longstanding involvement in Somalia’s political recovery. ‘Twin nation’ “Let those who do not know Djibouti learn about it, and let there be no miscalculation. Djibouti is Somalia, and Somalia is Djibouti,” he said. “We are two countries, but we are twin nations, bound by brotherhood, blood and shared ancestry.” A central part of Nur’s address focused on Djibouti’s contribution to Somalia’s state-building efforts following the collapse of the central government in 1991. He recalled how Djibouti hosted reconciliation initiatives aimed at bringing Somali factions together, ending violence and restoring national institutions. Nur singled out the historic Arta peace conference, which paved the way for the establishment of Somalia’s Transitional National Government in 2000. The conference marked a significant step in efforts to restore Somali state institutions and re-establish the country’s political representation internationally after years of civil conflict. “When Somalia’s central government collapsed in 1991, Djibouti stepped forward to bring Somalis together, stop the bloodshed and rebuild our state,” Nur said. He credited Djiboutian President Ismail Omar Guelleh with playing an important role in those efforts. “Somalia remembers the support Djibouti extended to our country and the role President Ismail Omar Guelleh played in the restoration of the Somali state,” he said. Longstanding friend Nur described Guelleh as a longstanding friend and supporter of Somalia, saying the Somali people would continue to recognise Djibouti’s contribution to their country’s recovery. He also praised Djibouti’s subsequent efforts to mediate political disagreements among Somali groups and encourage dialogue between opposing sides. “The debt of gratitude we owe Djibouti is one that we carry with us. It is written in the memory of the Somali people, and it is our responsibility to pass that history on to future generations,” he said. Fight against terrorism Nur also paid tribute to Djibouti’s military contribution to Somalia’s security, particularly the Djiboutian troops serving alongside Somali forces in operations against terrorist groups. He said Djibouti’s support had gone beyond hosting peace conferences and diplomatic engagement, extending to direct military assistance during the rebuilding of Somalia’s security institutions. “Djibouti did not limit its support to peace conferences and diplomatic efforts. You sent your sons to stand with us in the difficult fight against terrorism and in defence of the peace and lives of the Somali people,” he said. The speaker expressed particular appreciation for Djiboutian troops serving on the front lines in Somalia. RECOMMENDED Former Nigeria governor loses $136m wealth seizure appeal in corruption case Ebola outbreak: Kenya discharges more patients after recovery Uganda's former deputy army chief arrested over 'destabilisation' plot South Sudan to recruit 10,000 police officers ahead of first-ever polls RECOMMENDED Former Nigeria governor loses $136m wealth seizure appeal in corruption case Ebola outbreak: Kenya discharges more patients after recovery Uganda's former deputy army chief arrested over 'destabilisation' plot South Sudan to recruit 10,000 police officers ahead of first-ever polls “The Somali people see your courage, appreciate your sacrifices and will never forget your solidarity,” Nur said, addressing Djiboutian military officers and soldiers deployed in Somalia. He also praised Djibouti’s diplomatic support for Somalia’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity at regional and international forums. Nur said Djibouti had maintained those positions despite the political, diplomatic and security challenges involved. Regional tensions Turning to developments in the Horn of Africa, Nur warned that the region was facing increasing competition, security tensions and challenges affecting the stability of neighbouring countries. He said those circumstances required Somalia and Djibouti to strengthen consultations, coordinate their responses and maintain close cooperation. “Our region is passing through a difficult period. Competition is intensifying, security tensions are increasing, and circumstances are emerging that affect the stability of our countries and the lives of our people,” he said. “This moment demands wisdom, vigilance and greater unity. We need to consult one another, remain closely coordinated and work together to overcome the challenges ahead.” Nur reiterated that Somalia regarded Djibouti’s security as directly linked to its own, describing peace and stability in both countries as a common responsibility. His remarks highlighted the importance Mogadishu places on its relationship with Djibouti as regional governments confront security and diplomatic challenges. Parliamentary diplomacy The Somali speaker also outlined plans to deepen cooperation between the two countries’ parliaments. Nur said he had deliberately chosen Djibouti as the destination for his first official visit to a foreign parliament since becoming speaker of Somalia’s House of the People. “Beginning my official parliamentary visits in Djibouti was a deliberate choice, reflecting the affection, respect and recognition of the brotherly support that binds our two countries,” he said. “I wanted my first step to bring me to this parliament and this country, which has played such an important role in Somalia’s recovery.” He called for closer cooperation between parliamentary committees, greater exchanges of legislative expertise and joint training opportunities for parliamentary staff. “We want our committees to work together, our lawmakers to exchange experience, and the staff of our two parliaments to benefit from joint training and knowledge-sharing,” Nur said. The speaker also highlighted the importance of parliamentary diplomacy in strengthening relations between the two governments and creating opportunities for cooperation that benefit their populations. A relationship rooted in shared historyNur concluded his address by thanking Djibouti’s government, parliament and people for their hospitality and longstanding support for Somalia. He said his visit was intended not only to strengthen institutional relations but also to renew the bonds of solidarity between the two countries. “We have come to thank you. We have come to renew our bond of brotherhood. We have come to deliver a message from the Somali people: Somalia remembers Djibouti’s support,” he said. The speaker expressed hope that the relationship would continue to develop through practical cooperation between the two parliaments. For Somalia, Nur’s address placed Djibouti’s role in the country’s political reconstruction, military security and diplomatic engagement at the centre of a partnership he said must remain strong as the Horn of Africa faces new challenges. Speaking to Djibouti's parliament, he highlighted Djibouti's critical role in Somalia's rebuilding efforts, particularly through the historic Arta peace conference and military support against terrorism. Nur stated, "Djibouti’s security is our security, and Somalia’s security is Djibouti’s security," underscoring their shared responsibility for peace and stability. Nur called for enhanced cooperation between the two nations, particularly in parliamentary diplomacy, to strengthen their ties and address regional security challenges. The agreement was signed on Monday in Djibouti City by the Speaker of Somalia’s House of the People and the Speaker of Djibouti’s National Assembly, Dileita Mohamed Dileita. Under the agreement, the two parliaments will cooperate on improving legislative procedures, training parliamentary staff, conducting legal research and modernizing their institutional operations. The memorandum also provides for closer cooperation between parliamentary standing committees, the use of modern technology, improved data security and the establishment of parliamentary friendship groups between the two countries. Both sides also agreed to coordinate their positions on issues discussed at regional and international parliamentary forums. Following the signing ceremony, Dileita welcomed the outcome of discussions with the Somali delegation, saying the exchange of views had produced positive results for both countries. The Somali parliamentary speaker said Mogadishu was committed to strengthening ties with Djibouti through knowledge-sharing and institutional cooperation. The agreement is part of broader efforts by the two neighboring countries to expand bilateral relations and strengthen cooperation between their government institutions. somalia.title: African Union Somalia Bases Plan Follows Uganda Exit - https://kulu-media.com/
somalia.content: African Union Somalia Bases Plan Follows Uganda Exit | Kulu Media Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Connect with us Search Kulu Media African Union Plans to Secure Four Somalia Bases as Ugandan Troops Withdraw Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Home » News » Africa » Horn of Africa » African Union Plans to Secure Four Somalia Bases as Ugandan Troops Withdraw Horn of Africa African Union Plans to Secure Four Somalia Bases as Ugandan Troops Withdraw African Union peacekeepers prepare to secure four bases near Mogadishu. Published 52 seconds ago on November 3, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ugandan troops serving under the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) stand in formation as the mission's force commander inspects a guard of honour during a medal ceremony. File photo. Credit: AMISOM Public Information / Wikimedia Commons The African Union mission in Somalia plans to take control of four strategic military positions near Mogadishu as Ugandan troops withdraw from the country, according to newly reported details of an official mission letter. The move is intended to prevent Al-Shabaab militants from exploiting security gaps in southern Somalia. The African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) will redeploy peacekeepers to Sabiid-Anole, Bariire, Awdheegle and Bulonagad in the Lower Shabelle region during troop rotations scheduled for November 2026. According to an Associated Press report published on November 3, the plan was outlined in an October 31 letter from AUSSOM to the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS). The letter identifies the four positions as strategically important to Mogadishu’s security and proposes transferring African Union personnel from the coastal town of Barawe to reinforce them. The new arrangements follow Uganda’s decision to begin withdrawing troops deployed under a bilateral security agreement with Somalia, raising concerns about the ability of Somali and African Union forces to maintain control of areas previously secured by Ugandan units. As previously reported by Kulu Media , the African Union had warned that Uganda’s departure could leave parts of southern Somalia vulnerable to Al-Shabaab attacks. Four Strategic Positions Near Mogadishu The four positions identified for African Union control are located in Lower Shabelle, a region that has experienced repeated fighting between Somali government forces and Al-Shabaab militants. The October 31 letter describes the locations as critical to protecting Mogadishu and preventing militants from exploiting gaps created by the withdrawal of Uganda’s bilateral troops. AUSSOM intends to reposition personnel currently serving in the Barawe sub-sector, approximately 220 kilometers southwest of Mogadishu, to the four locations. A detailed account published by The Somali Digest on November 3 identifies the letter as reference AUSSOM/HOM/22/044.26. According to that account, AUSSOM asked UNSOS to recognize Sabiid-Anole, Bariire, Awdheegle and Bulonagad as new mission locations and continue providing logistical assistance to the redeployed peacekeepers. The request also calls for the Barawe sub-sector to be reclassified as locations outside the African Union mission’s operational structure. However, the letter does not specify which forces will assume responsibility for all the positions being vacated in Barawe. That uncertainty raises questions about whether the redeployment will strengthen defenses closer to Mogadishu while creating additional security responsibilities farther south. Uganda Begins Withdrawal Under Two Separate Arrangements Uganda announced on November 2 that it had begun withdrawing military personnel from Somalia, ending the first phase of a deployment that has supported counterinsurgency operations for nearly two decades. Ugandan military spokesperson Colonel Chris Magezi confirmed that the first group of troops had returned home and that personnel serving under the bilateral agreement were expected to complete their withdrawal within days. Uganda also contributes thousands of soldiers to AUSSOM, but those personnel are operating under a separate African Union mandate. The broader withdrawal of Ugandan forces, including its African Union peacekeeping contingent, is planned to proceed gradually through the end of 2027. A Reuters report confirmed that Uganda had begun its phased departure after almost 20 years of military involvement in Somalia. The October 31 AUSSOM letter explains that Uganda deployed additional bilateral troops following an April 2025 summit in Entebbe, where African leaders discussed strengthening security around Mogadishu. Those forces subsequently participated in operations to recover and hold territory previously controlled or contested by Al-Shabaab. The decision to withdraw the bilateral contingent has therefore required the African Union mission to reconsider how it distributes its remaining forces. Questions Remain Over Security in Barawe The proposed redeployment could create a difficult security transition in Barawe, a strategically important coastal town that Somali and African Union forces recovered from Al-Shabaab in 2014. The town is also the official capital of Somalia’s South West State. According to the Associated Press, Somali army commander Major General Ibrahim Mohamed Mohamud visited military personnel in Barawe on November 2 and instructed them to remain vigilant and intensify operations against Al-Shabaab. However, the army’s statement did not clarify whether Somali national forces would assume responsibility for all the African Union positions being vacated. The Somali Digest separately reported claims from local security sources that Ugandan troops had handed positions in Barawe and Shalanbood to Somali forces. Those reported handovers had not been officially confirmed by AUSSOM or Somalia’s federal government at the time of reporting. The distinction is important because the African Union’s plan to take over four positions near Mogadishu does not automatically establish that the security arrangements for Barawe and surrounding areas have been completed. Funding Shortages Complicate Security Transition The redeployment is taking place amid continuing financial and logistical challenges facing the African Union mission. Farhan Isak Yusuf, deputy executive director of the Mogadishu-based research organization Somali Public Agenda, told the Associated Press that funding shortages had contributed to the pressure surrounding Uganda’s withdrawal. He also warned that Somali national forces face resource limitations while confronting an insurgency that continues to threaten government-controlled territory. AUSSOM relies heavily on international assistance for transportation, fuel, medical evacuation, communications and other essential operational requirements. The October 31 letter specifically requests continued UNSOS logistical support for the four positions that the African Union intends to occupy. The mission’s financial difficulties have raised concerns about its ability to maintain existing deployments while supporting Somalia’s transition toward greater national responsibility for security. The issue also affects other countries contributing personnel to the African Union mission, including Ethiopia, whose military presence in Somalia remains important to regional counterinsurgency cooperation. Somalia has sought to maintain its neutral position amid growing tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Uganda’s decision is a separate development and should not be interpreted as confirmation that other troop-contributing countries have adopted similar withdrawal plans. Al-Shabaab Threat Remains a Central Concern Al-Shabaab, an Al-Qaeda-linked militant organization, continues to carry out attacks against Somali government forces, African Union troops and civilian targets. Lower Shabelle remains particularly important because of its proximity to Mogadishu and its network of roads connecting the capital to southern Somalia. The group’s ability to conduct attacks in contested areas has made the security transition especially sensitive. The African Union’s decision to reinforce four positions reflects concern that withdrawing experienced troops without suitable replacements could create opportunities for militants to regain influence. However, there has been no independently verified evidence that Al-Shabaab has captured the four positions as a direct result of Uganda’s latest withdrawal. Somalia is also dealing with political disagreements between federal authorities and regional administrations, adding pressure to the government’s efforts to coordinate security operations. The challenge is not limited to replacing departing troops. It also involves ensuring that Somali forces have sufficient personnel, equipment, logistical support and political coordination to maintain security over time. African Union Faces Difficult Decisions Over Remaining Forces The planned transfer of peacekeepers to Sabiid-Anole, Bariire, Awdheegle and Bulonagad represents an immediate operational response to Uganda’s withdrawal. It also illustrates the difficult choices facing AUSSOM as the mission attempts to protect strategic areas while preparing for a gradual reduction in foreign military involvement. The four positions are expected to receive African Union personnel during November’s troop rotations, but questions remain about the timing of the handovers, the future of the Barawe bases and the availability of continued international support. For Somalia, the outcome will depend on whether the redeployment successfully prevents security gaps without weakening other areas where Al-Shabaab remains active. The African Union’s latest plan offers a proposed solution for four strategically important positions, but it does not yet resolve the broader challenges surrounding Uganda’s military departure and Somalia’s long-term security transition. (AP Photo/Farah Abdi Warsameh, File) The African Union’s security mission in Somalia has warned that Uganda’s troop withdrawal could leave parts of southern Somalia vulnerable to attacks by Al-Shabaab, raising concerns about the future of counterinsurgency operations as Kampala begins ending nearly two decades of military involvement in the country. The warning was contained in an October 31 letter from the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) to the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS), according to a Reuters report published on November 2, 2026. Two diplomatic sources verified the letter, which identified potential security gaps in the Lower Shabelle region, where Ugandan troops have supported Somali forces in operations against the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group. The warning comes as Uganda confirms that its military has begun a phased withdrawal from Somalia, starting with troops deployed under a separate bilateral security agreement with the Somali government. Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) spokesperson Chris Magezi said the first contingent of soldiers had already returned home. The military confirmed that the withdrawal would eventually include Ugandan personnel serving under AUSSOM, with the entire process expected to be completed by the end of 2027. Uganda currently has approximately 4,500 troops deployed under the African Union mission, although the number of additional soldiers serving under bilateral arrangements has not been publicly established. African Union Raises Concerns Over Security Gaps The African Union mission’s warning highlights the risk that areas previously secured by Ugandan and Somali troops could become vulnerable if international forces leave before Somali security institutions are prepared to assume full responsibility. Lower Shabelle has been a major focus of military operations against Al-Shabaab, with Ugandan forces supporting efforts to recover strategic towns and disrupt militant positions. The region includes important routes connecting Mogadishu with other parts of southern Somalia, making its security particularly significant for the federal government’s counterinsurgency campaign. Ugandan forces have participated in operations around towns including Sabiid-Anole, Bariire and Awdhegle, where Somali authorities have sought to consolidate control following military offensives. However, maintaining security in recovered areas remains a challenge because Al-Shabaab continues to conduct attacks against government forces, African Union personnel and civilian targets. The AUSSOM letter identifies potential vulnerabilities resulting from the withdrawal. It does not establish that Al-Shabaab has launched a new offensive or captured additional territory following Uganda’s announcement. Uganda Confirms Phased Withdrawal After Nearly 20 Years Uganda first deployed troops to Somalia in 2007 as part of the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM), becoming one of the earliest and most significant contributors to international security operations in the country. Its forces helped push Al-Shabaab militants out of major urban areas, including parts of Mogadishu, and subsequently supported operations across southern Somalia. The mission evolved from AMISOM into the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) before AUSSOM began operations in January 2025. According to the Associated Press , Uganda’s military confirmed on November 2 that the first group of soldiers had returned home under the phased withdrawal arrangement. Thousands of Ugandan troops remain deployed, and their departure is expected to take place gradually rather than through an immediate removal of all personnel. The distinction between Uganda’s bilateral deployment and its African Union mission forces is important. The initial withdrawal affects troops deployed through the bilateral arrangement, while the broader plan also envisages the eventual departure of Uganda’s AUSSOM contingent. Somali State Minister for Foreign Affairs Ali Omar acknowledged the potential consequences of an abrupt withdrawal. Speaking to Reuters, Omar said the current situation was not critical but warned that a sudden departure of Ugandan troops could create security problems. His comments indicate concern about the timing and coordination of the transition rather than confirmation of an immediate collapse in security. Somalia Faces Growing Pressure to Assume Security Responsibilities Uganda’s withdrawal comes at a sensitive moment for Somalia, where the federal government is seeking to strengthen national security institutions while continuing its campaign against Al-Shabaab. The militant organization remains capable of carrying out bombings, ambushes and attacks on military and civilian targets despite years of operations by Somali forces and their international partners. The departure of experienced Ugandan units could increase pressure on Somali security forces to hold territory, protect major transport routes and prevent militants from exploiting security gaps. The transition is also taking place amid financial uncertainty surrounding international support for the African Union mission. In September, the United States agreed to provide additional time for the United Nations to wind down logistical assistance to AUSSOM, as previously reported by Kulu Media . That arrangement provides temporary relief but does not resolve the mission’s longer-term funding and logistical challenges. UNSOS supplies essential services, including transportation, fuel, medical assistance, communications and other operational support to African Union personnel and Somali security forces. Any reduction in troop numbers or logistical assistance could complicate security operations unless alternative arrangements are established. Political Divisions Complicate Somalia’s Security Transition The withdrawal also coincides with political disagreements between Somalia’s federal government and opposition groups over constitutional reforms, elections and the distribution of political authority. The closure of the United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia on October 31 has added to concerns about the country’s political transition. Although the political mission has ended, UN humanitarian agencies and separate logistical support arrangements remain active. Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has repeatedly emphasized the need for stronger national institutions and continued international cooperation against Al-Shabaab. In a recent interview with Sky News, covered by Kulu Media, Mohamud defended his government’s security strategy and discussed Somalia’s relationships with neighboring countries. He also reaffirmed that Somalia would remain outside any potential confrontation between Ethiopia and Eritrea, as detailed in Kulu Media’s report . The president has presented Somalia’s long-term security strategy as one combining military operations, efforts to counter extremist ideology and measures to disrupt militant financing. However, political divisions between federal and regional authorities could complicate the coordination required to maintain security as international forces gradually withdraw. Withdrawal Raises Questions About Future Operations Against Al-Shabaab Uganda’s planned departure represents a significant transition for Somalia’s security architecture after almost two decades of military cooperation. The African Union’s warning underscores concerns that a poorly coordinated withdrawal could weaken security in areas where Al-Shabaab remains active. For Somalia, the central challenge will be ensuring that national forces can assume responsibility for areas currently protected by international troops without creating opportunities for militant groups to regain influence. The timetable extends through the end of 2027, giving Somali authorities, Uganda and the African Union time to coordinate the transition. However, the effectiveness of that process will depend on the readiness of Somali security forces, continued logistical support and political cooperation between the country’s institutions. No new Al-Shabaab territorial gains directly resulting from Uganda’s withdrawal had been independently confirmed at the time of reporting. somalia.summary: The African Union (AU) plans to secure four military bases in Somalia as Ugandan troops begin their withdrawal, which raises concerns about potential security gaps that could be exploited by Al-Shabaab militants. The bases, located near Mogadishu in the Lower Shabelle region, are critical for maintaining security in the area. The African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) intends to redeploy peacekeepers to Sabiid-Anole, Bariire, Awdheegle, and Bulonagad during troop rotations scheduled for November 2026. Uganda's withdrawal, which has been ongoing since November 2, marks the end of nearly two decades of military involvement in Somalia. The AU has warned that this departure could leave southern Somalia vulnerable to attacks. The transition is complicated by financial and logistical challenges faced by AUSSOM, raising questions about the ability of Somali forces to maintain security in the absence of Ugandan troops. The situation underscores the ongoing threat posed by Al-Shabaab and the need for effective coordination among Somali and AU forces.

Security Threats About ADF Contact Subscription Contribute Archive English Français العربية Português English Français العربية Português Home » Daily News » Somalia Faces Critical Security Challenges Daily News Somalia Faces Critical Security Challenges Al-Shabaab pressure persists amid diminished international support, political friction in Somalia By ADF November 3, 2026 4 Mins Read Somali National Army Soldiers patrol near Sabiid, a town liberated from al-Shabaab. [AFP/GETTY IMAGES] Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Email Reddit WhatsApp Copy Link Somalia faces a convergence of crises, including the departure of international forces, persistent terror threats from al-Shabaab, political division and regional tension, that leave it on the precipice of chaos. On August 8, Ethiopian forces serving under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) handed over a military base to the Somali National Army in the southern town of Burhakaba. Ethiopian troops had maintained a presence at the base since 2014. Now Somali troops must address security concerns posed by al-Shabaab and other armed groups on its own. Analysts question whether Somalia has the capacity to do so, especially amid diminishing international support. “The issue is not whether Ethiopian forces should remain indefinitely. Nor is it whether Somali sovereignty is negotiable,” analyst Abdi Guled wrote for the Horn Briefs newsletter. “The issue is whether the state taking responsibility for a position possesses the logistics, intelligence, reinforcement capacity and political legitimacy to keep it.” The handover in Burhakaba occurred amid ongoing political friction between Ethiopia and Somalia over sovereignty issues related to the breakaway region of Somaliland. It also happened as the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) faces severe funding cuts, including at least $500 million in international support that will be cut off by December 31, 2026. UNSOS supports approximately 12,000 AUSSOM personnel and as many as 20,900 Somali security personnel. It funds food, water, fuel, transportation, medical evacuation, communications, engineering, maintenance and other critical battlefield services. In August, the agency said it moved about 240 tons of food each month to sectors and forward operating bases around the country. Observers wonder how such deliveries will be made come January. “A soldier at a remote base does not experience an international funding mechanism as a diplomatic abstraction. He experiences it as fuel arriving, or not arriving,” Guled wrote. “As food supplies being delivered. As a helicopter available for medical evacuation. As a vehicle that still works. As ammunition reaching a position before an attack rather than afterward. For much of the post-2006 period, those functions have been heavily supported by the international system.” Mohamed Daud Ismail, a senior research assistant at the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) project, believes this shortfall will leave the approximately 12,000-strong AUSSOM force “operationally unsustainable.” “Without immediate alternative international funding, AUSSOM faces imminent operational collapse heading into 2027,” Ismail wrote. “Because the Somali National Army (SNA) remains overstretched and structurally unequipped to manage complex country-wide logistics independently, an abrupt degradation of African Union positions will trigger an immediate, destabilizing security vacuum across central and southern Somalia.” Ismail predicted that al-Shabaab will try to exploit security gaps with a major offensive throughout the final months of 2026 and into 2027. “This push could allow the group to reclaim territorial footholds in the central and southern regions while directly threatening major urban hubs, including Mogadishu and Kismayo,” Ismail wrote. As Somali troops lose direct battlefield assistance, the country also lost assistance from the United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) at the end of October. As that date approached, Hassan Moallim Mohamud, Somalia’s minister of justice and constitutional affairs, thanked UNTMIS delegates for supporting justice sector institutions, particularly in capacity-building, legal and policy development, and corrections reform. As with battlefield concerns, analysts question whether Somalia can maintain any momentum UNTMIS helped establish. The end of UNTMIS “raises the central question that has accompanied every phase of the UN’s engagement in Somalia: can national institutions sustain and build on the gains achieved with international support?” wrote researchers with FTL Somalia, a policy and research institute. Mohamud’s justice and constitutional affairs office will now handle UNTMIS-related work on its own. “The handover to the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs, with continued backing from UNDP [United Nations Development Program] and UNODC [United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime], suggests a phased approach that recognises national capacity remains a work in progress,” FTL Somalia researchers wrote. The funding cuts, troop drawdowns and the end of UNTMIS coincide with ​armed resistance from state governments upset over Mogadishu’s influence over state elections. Some states have rejected constitutional changes they say leave power with the federal government. “Somalia does not necessarily face an imminent collapse,” Guled wrote. “It faces something more difficult to measure and potentially more consequential: the gradual erosion of the infrastructure that has made the country’s security system viable. And that erosion is occurring at the same time that the country’s political order is becoming less cohesive.” national security Somalia Terrorism Share. somalia.summary: Somalia is grappling with severe security challenges as international support dwindles, political divisions deepen, and threats from the militant group al-Shabaab persist. The recent handover of a military base from Ethiopian forces to the Somali National Army (SNA) in Burhakaba highlights the urgent need for Somalia to independently manage its security. Analysts express concern over the SNA's capacity to handle these responsibilities, especially with significant funding cuts to the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) looming. This reduction could lead to operational collapse for the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), which relies on international aid for essential services. As Somali troops lose battlefield assistance, the potential for al-Shabaab to exploit security gaps increases, threatening major urban centers like Mogadishu. The situation is further complicated by regional tensions and dissatisfaction among state governments regarding federal influence, raising questions about the sustainability of Somalia's security and political infrastructure.

somalia.title: AUSSOM commander meets Hirshabelle leader amid tensions with Hiiraan region authorities - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: AUSSOM commander meets Hirshabelle leader amid tensions with Hiiraan region authorities - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS AUSSOM commander meets Hirshabelle leader amid tensions with Hiiraan region authorities Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Monday November 2, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) – The commander of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) Sector 5, Brig. Gen. Michel Ndenzako, met with Hirshabelle State President Ali Abdullahi Hussein Guudlawe in Jowhar on Sunday, with talks focusing on security coordination and information sharing. The meeting, held at Villa Hirshabelle, brought together the two officials to discuss cooperation between AUSSOM, Somali security forces and local authorities. Guudlawe commended the AUSSOM Burundi National Defence Force (BNDF) contingent for its continued support in protecting state institutions and strategic infrastructure. Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to closer coordination and joint efforts to protect critical infrastructure, strengthen security and promote lasting peace and stability in Hirshabelle State. The meeting comes amid a dispute between the Hirshabelle administration and local authorities in the Hiiraan region over administrative control and authority. Mohamed Hussein Mohamed, the governor of Hiiraan, recently rejected a decision by the Hirshabelle administration to dismiss him. In a statement issued days ago, he instructed airlines not to transport individuals affiliated with the Hirshabelle administration. The dispute has also affected customs operations. Mohamed announced the closure of a customs checkpoint in Matabaan, where taxes had previously been collected, and said operations had been moved to a newly established checkpoint in the El-Gal area. (Photo: Somaliland Presidency / Handout) SHARE Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Mogadishu (Somalia Today) — Somalia on Tuesday rejected the accreditation of Israel’s first ambassador to breakaway Somaliland and the laying of an embassy foundation stone in Hargeisa, saying both violated its sovereignty. The foreign ministry said the steps had been taken without the federal government’s consent and declared them “null and void and without legal effect”. Israel’s foreign ministry said Sunday that Michael Lotem had presented his credentials to Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi the previous week. A foundation stone for the planned embassy was laid after the ceremony, the ministry said. Israel recognised Somaliland on December 26, 2025, becoming the first United Nations member state to recognise its independence since its 1991 break with Somalia. It remains the only UN member to have done so. Mogadishu demanded that Israel reverse the measures. It urged other governments and international organisations to reject them and avoid engagement that could legitimise the moves. It said it reserved the right to pursue diplomatic, political and legal measures under international law. “The unity of the Somali nation is not negotiable,” the ministry said . The Arab League condemned the developments on Monday. Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy said they violated Somalia’s territorial integrity and accused Israel of exploiting divisions in the country to expand its military and political influence near the Gulf of Aden. Exchange of ambassadors The Israeli foreign ministry said the exchange of ambassadors fulfilled an agreement reached when the two sides recognised one another. “Israel is determined to develop and strengthen its relations with Somaliland,” Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said in Sunday’s announcement . Sa’ar visited Hargeisa in January, while Somaliland opened an embassy in Jerusalem during Abdullahi’s visit to Israel in June, according to the Israeli foreign ministry. Its statement gave no opening date for the Hargeisa embassy. Somaliland’s presidency hailed the ceremony as a milestone marking “the strengthening of diplomatic ties and the implementation of strategic cooperation between the two countries and two peoples”. Abdullahi called for practical cooperation in trade, investment, infrastructure, security and technology, according to Somaliland’s foreign ministry. The Israeli envoy affirmed that he would work to turn shared goals into “concrete gains that benefit both sides”, specifically in the areas of security, defence, trade, technology, healthcare and education. Sovereignty dispute Somaliland has governed itself for more than three decades, maintaining its own institutions, security forces and currency. Somalia’s federal government says the territory remains part of the country and has no authority to establish diplomatic relations independently. The former British protectorate became independent in June 1960 before uniting with the formerly Italian-administered territory to form the Somali Republic. Somaliland’s leaders say their 1991 declaration restored that earlier sovereignty. Somaliland’s foreign ministry rejected foreign criticism of the envoy’s appointment in April, calling recognition “a grounded legal reality, not a matter of political convenience”. It said Somaliland determines its own foreign relations. In Tuesday’s statement, Mogadishu cited the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations . Article 2 says diplomatic relations between states and permanent diplomatic missions are established by mutual consent. “No unilateral act can circumvent that requirement or alter the status of Somali territory,” the Somali ministry said. The African Union does not recognise Somaliland as an independent state. In April, the AU Commission condemned Israel’s decision to appoint an envoy and reaffirmed its support for Somalia’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity. Somaliland lies on the Gulf of Aden, across from Yemen and near the approaches to the Bab el-Mandeb strait, a major shipping passage linking the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean. Tuesday’s statement also warned of wider risks amid heightened insecurity around the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. “Actions that encourage fragmentation and disregard internationally recognised borders risk deepening tensions across an already fragile region,” the ministry said. Ayaan Abdullahi Ayaan Abdullahi reports on Somalia and Somalis for Somalia Today. Based in Mogadishu, she has more than five years of experience covering current affairs and major developments affecting Somali communities. somalia.summary: Somalia has officially rejected the accreditation of Israel's first ambassador to the self-declared independent region of Somaliland, as well as the establishment of an Israeli embassy in Hargeisa. The Somali foreign ministry stated that these actions were taken without the federal government's consent and declared them "null and void." Israel recognized Somaliland's independence in December 2025, becoming the first UN member to do so. In response, Somalia urged Israel to reverse these measures and called on other nations to refrain from legitimizing them. The Arab League also condemned the developments, asserting they violated Somalia's territorial integrity. Somaliland, which has operated independently since 1991, maintains its own governance and security but is not recognized as a separate state by the African Union or Somalia's federal government. The Somali ministry emphasized that diplomatic relations require mutual consent, warning that actions undermining recognized borders could exacerbate regional tensions.

football.summary: تستعرض يلاكورة مواعيد ونتائج مباريات دوري أبطال أفريقيا لموسم 2026/2027، حيث يتضمن جدول المباريات مجموعة من المواجهات المثيرة. من المقرر أن تبدأ الجولة الأولى من دور الـ32 في 22 يناير 2027، حيث يلتقي الهلال السوداني مع المغرب الفاسي، وسيمبا مع نادي كولومب، بالإضافة إلى مباريات أخرى تشمل الزمالك ضد مولودية الجزائر والترجي الرياضي ضد إف سي نواذيبو. كما يتم تسليط الضوء على الفرق المشاركة مثل الأفريقي التونسي، المريخ، والهلال السوداني، مع تقديم إحصائيات حول الهدافين وصانعي الأهداف. تتضمن المقالة أيضًا أخبارًا تتعلق بالفرق، مثل تعثر الأفريقي أمام الملعب التونسي، واستعدادات الزمالك لمواجهاته المقبلة. يهدف الموقع إلى توفير معلومات شاملة حول البطولة، بما في ذلك التحليلات والتقارير المتعلقة بالمباريات والفرق.

football.content: المريخ يربك تحضيرات الهلال لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا المريخ يربك تحضيرات الهلال لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا مباريات اليوم من ديربي السودان الكبير بين الغريمين الهلال والمريخ (winwin) 3 نوفمبر 2026 المريخ يربك تحضيرات الهلال لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا الهلال السوداني المريخ دوري أبطال أفريقيا الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin عاد نجم نادي الهلال والمنتخب السوداني، مصطفى كرشوم، إلى الواجهة بقوة، مقدمًا مستويات مميزة في الآونة الأخيرة، إذ استعاد بريقه الكامل خلال مباراتي "صقور الجديان" في التصفيات الأفريقية، ومباريات فريقه في الدورين التمهيديين لمسابقة دوري أبطال أفريقيا . وقد أشعل المدافع المتألق سباقًا مبكرًا بين قطبي الكرة السودانية مع اقتراب دخوله "الفترة الحرة"، إذ يسعى النادي الأحمر لاستعادة نجمه السابق، بينما يتمسك "الأزرق" بجوهرته بعد أن وجد ضالته في المدافع الفذ، الذي يصنفه الخبراء بأنه أفضل لاعب في البلاد خلال السنوات الأخيرة. الهلال يتحرك للحفاظ على نجمه في هذا السياق، كشفت مصادر موثوقة لموقع "winwin" أن إدارة نادي الهلال استشعرت الخطر، وبدأت تحركاتها مبكرًا لتأمين بقاء نجمها وتمديد تعاقده قبل دخوله الفترة الحرة؛ وذلك بعد أن نجح اللاعب في إعادة الصلابة والهيبة لدفاع الفريق، الذي عانى من تذبذب واضح في مستوياته السابقة. ويعد كرشوم ظاهرة نادرة في الملاعب السودانية؛ نظرًا لسلوكه الاحترافي وانضباطه العالي، فضلًا عن ثبات مستواه وقلة أخطائه. وفي هذا الصدد، فتحت إدارة النادي برئاسة هشام السوباط باب التفاوض مع اللاعب؛ لضمان استمراره في صفوف الفريق لمدة عامين إضافيين على الأقل. اقرأ أيضًا اكتسح الترشيحات.. نجم الهلال السوداني يقترب من تتويج خاص خاص | نجم السودان يفتح النار ويشرح أسباب خيبة المريخ قاريًا وكشفت مصادر عالية الثقة، أنّ إدارة المريخ تعتزم استعادة نجمها، استجابة للمطالبات الجماهيرية الملحة، ونظرًا لقيمته الفنية العالية؛ إذ تعد عودته مكسبًا مضاعفًا باعتباره أفضل مدافع في البلاد، وسيشكل football.summary: تواجه الهلال السوداني فريق بيراميدز في مباراة ضمن دوري أبطال إفريقيا، حيث انتهت المباراة بالتعادل السلبي 0-0. أقيمت المباراة في 8 يناير 2027، وهي جزء من مرحلة المجموعات للموسم 2026/2027. يتواجد الهلال السوداني في المجموعة A، التي تضم أيضًا الترجي الرياضي التونسي وبيترو أتلتيكو ونواذيبو. على الرغم من عدم تسجيل أي أهداف، إلا أن المباراة كانت مثيرة، حيث حاول كلا الفريقين السيطرة على مجريات اللعب. الهلال السوداني يسعى لاستعادة توازنه بعد سلسلة من النتائج المتباينة في الدوري الرواندي، بينما بيراميدز يأمل في تحسين أدائه في البطولة. تتواصل المنافسات في دوري أبطال إفريقيا، حيث يتطلع كل فريق لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية في المباريات القادمة لتعزيز فرصه في التأهل إلى الأدوار المتقدمة.
